summary: Asks for the character set koi8-r, used for Cyrillic text on Unix systems and networks in the former Soviet Union, to be registered. The memo argues that its large user community makes registration worthwhile, even though it is not an international standard.

plainLanguage.summary: This memo describes koi8-r, a character set used for Cyrillic text, and gives a table mapping its upper-half codes to Unicode. It presents the name for MIME use and the background for its proposed registration.

subtitle: A registration request and character mapping for the koi8-r Cyrillic character set.

tldr.problem: The memo says a large community used koi8-r for Cyrillic text even though the character set was not an international standard.
tldr.mechanism: It gives the MIME character-set name koi8-r and a mapping of its upper-half codes to Unicode characters.
tldr.outcome: The document presents the encoding and its character table as support for registration. It is informational and does not itself describe mail transport procedures.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 1489 as Informational and records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The memo documents the koi8-r character mapping and requests registration.

sections.title: Why Describe koi8-r
sections.content:
The memo says koi8-r was not an international standard but had a large user community, including Relcom Net. It describes the encoding as a de facto standard for Unix and global network applications in the former Soviet Union.

The memo gives the MIME character-set name koi8-r and says the encoding was based on earlier standards and variations, including GOST 19768-74 (old-koi8), ISO 6937/8, INIS-cyrillic, and ISO 5427.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors document a character set already used by a substantial community. They provide its name for use in MIME messages.

sections.title: Mapping the Character Table
sections.content:
The lower half of the koi8-r code table coincides with ASCII. The RFC provides a C-language array mapping the upper 128 code positions to Unicode (ISO 10646) values.

The upper half includes Cyrillic letters, box-drawing characters, and symbols such as the square root and division sign. A separate list describes the characters associated with codes in that range.
sections.plainLanguage: The first half matches ASCII. The memo lists how each code in the upper half maps to a Cyrillic letter or another symbol.

sections.title: Scope and Character Descriptions
sections.content:
The RFC includes detailed names for the upper-half characters, including lowercase and uppercase Cyrillic letters, line-drawing forms, and mathematical symbols. This table makes the encoding's assignments explicit for readers and implementers.

The memo says it provides information to support registration of the character set. Its security section says security issues are not discussed.
sections.plainLanguage: The character list lets readers identify what each upper-half code means. This memo describes the encoding rather than defining an email protocol.
